newsitem.title: GERMANY: Veba, RWE, C&W confident in new telecoms alliance.
newsitem.headline: Veba, RWE, C&W confident in new telecoms alliance.

text.p: Germany's two largest utilities, RWE AG and Veba AG, and British-based Cable and Wireless said on Wednesday they will merge their telecommunications activities and create a powerful rival to monopoly Deutsche Telekom.

In one of the most far-reaching alliances to date and major realignment on the German telecommunications market, RWE and Veba will merge their entire communications networks into a new company and create another company to provide services.

The announcement follows the surprise defection of RWE from a previous alliance with British Telecom and Bavarian utility Viag AG that had been considered a promising challenger to Deutsche Telekom after telecoms deregulation in 1998.
That alliance fell apart over differences in strategy and control of some of the company's subsidiaries.

RWE chairman Dietmar Kuhnt, speaking to reporters in Essen late on Wednesday, said there had been insurmountable differences with Viag and BT over how to market the E2 mobile phone licence the companies were preparing to bid for.
But he indicated that RWE was frustrated by BT's strategy for Germany, which is restricted to the business market.

"Only powerful alliances with a broad and comprehensive product offering will survive," he said. "Not just a select group of large customers, but the broad population should benefit from the opening of the telecommunications market."
Kuhnt and Veba chairman Ulrich Hartmann said talks between the two companies had been underway for about a month.
Their agreement sees Vebacom, the joint venture between Veba and Cable and Wireless, taking 51 percent of the new service company, called Servco, and 49 percent of the network company, dubbed Netco.
A holding company called RWECOM will be created in which RWE will hold 75 percent and Vebacom 25 percent. RWECOM in turn will hold 51 percent of Netco and 49 percent of Servco.
As a result of this complex web of ownership, Veba will hold 40 percent of the new alliance, while RWE will hold 37.5 percent, leaving 22.5 percent for Cable and Wireless.
Vebacom and RWE will control the two companies through a joint management company, which will be located in Duesseldorf.

Vebacom will put its 37.5 percent stake in the E-Plus mobile phone group and its cable television activities in Servco. RWE and Veba will merge their entire communications networks into Netco. Correcting an earlier figure published by the company, Hartmann said Vebacom's contribution to the venture would be valued at 4.8 billion marks.
RWE's contribution, a combination of material assets and cash, would total around 3.6 billion marks.
Hartmann said the Veba's strategic alliance with Cable and Wireless -- it owns 10.5 percent of the British-based company -- was the only such alliance in Germany to have "stood the test of time".

"The new alliance of Veba, Cable and Wireless and RWE distinguishes itself as the only one in Germany that can offer an entire spectrum of telecommunications services -- from fixed-wire to cable TV and mobile communications," he said.

The new alliance creates a powerful competitor not only to Deutsche Telekom, but also to the DBKom alliance of Mannesmann AG, the German railway Deutsche Bahn AG and AT&T Corp, which has been considered the strongest of the newcomers.

Mannesmann, which owns Germany's D2 mobile phone network, plans to create a national telecommunications network by laying cable along the railway tracks. The railway already operates the second largest network after Deutsche Telekom.
While it is still uncertain how the new alliance will shape up in comparison to DBKom, Mannesmann and AT&T have now received serious competition from another newcomer.
"The new allinace, in my view, will be the leading competitor in Europe's biggest national market," said Richard Brown, the chief executive of Cable and Wireless, in London.
"This transaction underscores the value of our investment in Germany, materially reduces our exposure to start-up losses and will favourably impact our earnings, cash and balance sheet," he added.
A British Telecom spokesman called RWE's defection a "hiccup" in its plans for Germany.

"We're going alone (with Viag) for the fourth mobile phone licence in Germany -- but obviously we'll need some additional partners -- maybe on the infrastructure side or maybe on the equity side (in the longer term)," the spokesman said.
BT's European director Patrick Gallagher was also due to address the news conference.
Viag and BT will seek the fourth German E2 mobile telephone licence, which the Postal Ministry will grant in February 1997.

The group will create 9,000 new jobs by 2001, Obermeier said. Viag and BT aim for a share of 20 percent of the German mobile phone market and seven percent of the fixed-line market, he said, without giving target dates.

RWE's defection from the group on Wednesday to a rival alliance with Cable and Wireless Plc and utility VEBA AG appeared to leave BT weakened in Germany, particularly amid speculation that Viag could form closer ties to the RWE-Veba group.
RWE dropped out of the alliance with Viag and BT over differences in strategy and control of some of the company's subsidiaries.
Vebacom, the joint venture between Veba and Cable & Wireless, will take 51 percent of a new service company, called Servco, and 49 percent of a network company dubbed Netco.
RWE's contribution, a combination of material assets and cash, would total around 3.6 billion marks ($2.4 billion) , while Vebacom's contribution to the venture will be 4.8 billion marks.

A holding company called RWECOM will be created in which RWE will hold 75 percent and Vebacom 25 percent. RWECOM in turn will hold 51 percent of Netco and 49 percent of Servco. The new alliance creates a powerful competitor not only to Deutsche Telekom AG , but also to the DBKom alliance of Mannesmann AG, the German railway Deutsche Bahn AG and AT&T Corp, which has been considered the strongest of the newcomers.
